title: The field of dharma
hookLine: a blind king asks what happened on the field, and a man with borrowed sight begins to tell him
carry: every life is a field of dharma

lines: CAMP FOUR: ONE BOOK, IN ORDER.
cards: The Bhagavad Gita's first voice isn't Krishna's or Arjuna's. It's an old blind king, far from the battle, asking a question.
In Edwin Arnold's translation from 1885: "Ranged thus for battle on the sacred plain— On Kurukshetra—say, Sanjaya! say What wrought my people, and the Pandavas?"
Camp four is that book, the Song of the Lord, read in order over eleven weeks. Eighteen chapters; tradition counts seven hundred verses.
You met its people in the stories: the Pandava brothers, their cousins the Kauravas, Krishna taking the reins of Arjuna's chariot on the eve of war. The Gita begins right there.

teach.h: A REPORT TO A BLIND FATHER.
teach.b: The king is Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas. He can't see, and he isn't on the field. The sage Vyasa has given his minister, Sanjaya, the sight to see the whole battle from the palace.
So the entire Gita is a report, told to a blind father who already fears the answer. His first words: Dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah.

On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight. Two names at once: a real place, Kurukshetra, north of Delhi, where pilgrims still go, and dharmakshetra, the field of dharma.
Dharma is one of Hinduism's biggest words: what's right, the duty that's yours, the order that holds the world together. And listen to how the king asks: what did my sons do, and Pandu's?
Mine, and theirs. Many teachers hear his real blindness there. Sanjaya begins.

Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, walks up to his old teacher Drona and lists warriors, ours and theirs, a little too fast. Then old Bhishma, the great-uncle, roars like a lion to cheer him and blows his conch shell.
The whole field answers: conches, drums, horns, all at once. On the other side, in a great chariot yoked to white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blow theirs. Krishna's is Panchajanya.

teach.h: EVERY LIFE IS A FIELD OF DHARMA.
teach.b: Gandhi and many others have read that field as a human life: every life is a field of dharma, where you have to choose what's right while the noise is deafening and nobody has moved yet.

how: Many Hindus read or chant the Bhagavad Gita at home or in study groups, often a chapter at a time; the whole text is framed as Sanjaya's report to the blind king Dhritarashtra, and chapter one opens on the field of Kurukshetra.

games.q: the Gita's first verse names the place twice: Kurukshetra, and dharmakshetra. what does the second name tell you?
o: it's a field of dharma: a place where what's right has to be chosen.
it's the old name of a nearby city.
only priests were allowed to fight there.
games.why: dharmakshetra, the field of dharma. many Hindus read it as every life: the place where you choose what's right.

practice: Picture a wide plain at dawn, lined up with the things you're facing right now: a decision, a person, a deadline, a fear.
Let the noise come, the conches and drums and every voice in your head at once, and don't fight it; just hear it.
Underneath, notice your breath, still going, steady, like Sanjaya quietly telling what he sees: nobody has to move yet.
